requirements: Reproduce the neural topology optimization design, fabrication, and characterization of pentagonal photonic crystal lightsail mirrors as reported in the paper.

sub_tasks.requirements: Set up the computational environment including RCWA solver, neural network framework, L-BFGS optimizer, and physical constants required for lightsail simulation.
Provide software dependencies and environment configuration necessary for the neural topology optimization pipeline.

Code has been implemented that declares a reproducible Python environment (e.g., requirements.txt, environment.yml, or pyproject.toml) listing all dependencies needed for RCWA simulation, neural network reparameterization, and gradient-based optimization.

Code has been implemented that installs and imports an automatic-differentiation framework (e.g., JAX, PyTorch, or TensorFlow) capable of backpropagating gradients through the RCWA solver into the neural network parameters.

Code has been implemented that installs and imports an RCWA (Rigorous Coupled-Wave Analysis) solver library (e.g., grcwa, S4, or an equivalent differentiable RCWA implementation) suitable for computing reflection spectra of periodic 2D dielectric structures.

Code has been implemented that imports NLopt (or an equivalent library exposing the Method of Moving Asymptotes) so that the pixel-based MMA baseline referenced in Supplementary Section E can be executed alongside the neural TO pipeline.
Provide the RCWA solver interface used to evaluate reflectivity of candidate photonic crystal unit cells.

Code has been implemented that wraps the RCWA solver in a callable function taking a per-pixel permittivity grid, unit-cell period Lambda, layer thickness t, wavelength lambda, and polarization angle phi, and returning the zero-order (and total) reflectivity of a periodic single-layer SiN-like slab in vacuum.
The RCWA wrapper accepts both square (N x N) and hexagonal (N x sqrt(3) N) unit-cell geometries as described in the Methods section (Fig. 7), using appropriate lattice vectors for each case.

Code has been implemented that supports evaluating the RCWA solver at two orthogonal polarization angles phi = 0 and phi = pi/2 and averaging/combining the resulting reflectivities for use in the polarization-invariant FOM.

Code has been implemented that exposes the RCWA reflectivity as a differentiable function so that gradients of a scalar figure of merit with respect to the permittivity grid, Lambda, and t can be propagated back through the solver.
Provide the L-BFGS optimizer and iteration-control infrastructure used to update the CNN weights and auxiliary variables.

Code has been implemented that instantiates an L-BFGS optimizer (Nocedal 1980) to update both the trainable CNN weights/biases and the input latent vector beta, following the neural TO scheme of Hoyer et al. (2019).
Code has been implemented that runs the optimization loop until either a pre-set relative tolerance on the FOM or a maximum number of iterations is reached, as specified in the Methods section.
Define the physical and mission constants required by the RCWA simulations and figure-of-merit evaluations.

Code has been implemented that defines material constants for SiN with density rho_SiN = 3100 kg/m^3 and relative permittivity epsilon_SiN = 4, and vacuum with epsilon_vac = 1, matching the values stated in the Methods section.

Code has been implemented that sets the design-variable bounds thickness 0.01 um <= t <= 1 um and period 0.1 um <= Lambda <= 7.2 um, and the initial values t_0 = 100 nm and Lambda_0 = lambda_0 = 1.55 um, as specified in the Methods section.

Code has been implemented that defines the speed of light c and provides a helper computing the Doppler-shifted wavelength lambda(beta) = lambda_0 * sqrt((1+beta)/(1-beta)) so that reflectivity is evaluated across the operating band 1.55–1.86 um.
Encode the Starshot mission parameters (laser wavelength 1.55 µm, intensity 10 GW/m², 10 m² sail area, 1 g payload) and SiN material properties (density 3100 kg/m³, εr = 4) used throughout the study.
Mission constants for laser propulsion are encoded so downstream optimization and evaluation code consumes canonical Starshot values.

Code has been implemented that defines the propulsion laser wavelength λ₀ as a named constant equal to 1.55 µm (1.55e-6 m) and exposes it to the acceleration figure-of-merit and RCWA reflectivity evaluation routines.
Code has been implemented that defines the propulsion laser intensity I as 10 GW/m² (1e10 W/m²) as a named constant used in the acceleration distance D and acceleration time T computations.

Code has been implemented that defines the total illuminated sail area A as 10 m² and the payload (satellite) mass m_s as 1 g (1e-3 kg), used to compute payload area density ρ_s = m_s / A in the figure-of-merit formulas.

Code has been implemented that encodes the Doppler-shifted operating bandwidth for lightsail evaluation, mapping β=v/c ∈ [0, 0.2] to laser-frame wavelength λ(β) = λ₀·√((1+β)/(1−β)), yielding a swept wavelength range from 1.55 µm to approximately 1.86 µm.
The upper end of the Doppler-shifted wavelength range produced by the encoded mission parameters (β=0.2, λ₀=1.55 µm) matches 1.86 µm.

Code has been implemented that models the propulsion beam as a linearly polarized plane wave at normal incidence and evaluates the sail at two orthogonal polarization angles φ = 0 and φ = π/2 (averaging or jointly optimizing over both) as specified in the Methods.
SiN material properties are encoded consistently for both mass computations and electromagnetic (RCWA) simulations.
Code has been implemented that defines the SiN mass density ρ_SiN as 3100 kg/m³ and uses it to compute the sail area density ρ_l from the PhC thickness t and Area fraction A_f.

Code has been implemented that defines the SiN relative permittivity ε_r = 4 (refractive index n = 2) and vacuum permittivity ε_vac = 1, and passes these as the two-material palette to the RCWA solver so that design pixels are continuously varied between ε = 1 and ε = 4.

Code has been implemented that treats SiN optical absorption as negligible (ppm-level) in the D and T evaluation, so that any non-reflected power is accounted for as transmission in the acceleration integrals (matching the assumption stated in Fig. 3b).
Optimization variable bounds tied to mission/material scales are enforced.

Code has been implemented that constrains the PhC layer thickness t to 0.01 µm ≤ t ≤ 1 µm and the unit-cell period Λ to 0.1 µm ≤ Λ ≤ 7.2 µm during optimization, with initial thickness set to 100 nm and initial period set to λ₀ = 1.55 µm.

Implement the acceleration distance D (Eq. 1) and acceleration time T (Eq. 2) figures of merit including Doppler-shifted reflectivity integration and relativistic kinematics for lightsail optimization.
Doppler-shift relations and velocity kinematics used inside both figures of merit are implemented as reusable primitives.

Code has been implemented for the Doppler red-shift relation lambda(beta) = lambda_0 * sqrt((1+beta)/(1-beta)), mapping the rest-frame laser wavelength lambda_0 to the sail-frame wavelength as a function of beta = v/c.
The Doppler function returns lambda_0 when beta = 0 and returns 1.86 um (within 1 nm) when beta = 0.2 and lambda_0 = 1.55 um, matching the operating bandwidth 1.55-1.86 um stated in the Methods.
Code has been implemented for the Lorentz factor gamma(beta) = 1/sqrt(1 - beta^2) used in the acceleration-time integrand of Eq. 2.
Code has been implemented for the kinematic weighting function h(beta) = beta / ((1 - beta)^2 * sqrt(1 - beta^2)) used in the acceleration-distance integrand of Eq. 1.
Reflectivity R(lambda) sampling and polarization averaging that feed the FOM integrals are implemented.

Code has been implemented that exposes reflectivity R as a callable function of wavelength lambda over the Doppler bandshift range [lambda_0, lambda_0*sqrt((1+beta_f)/(1-beta_f))], driven by the RCWA solver applied to the current PhC unit-cell design.

Code has been implemented so that the R(lambda) entering the FOM is the average of the RCWA reflectivity for the two orthogonal linear polarizations phi = 0 and phi = pi/2, matching the polarization-invariant optimization described in the Methods.
The reflectivity used during optimization is evaluated at 24 wavelength points across the Doppler-shift interval, as specified in Supplementary Section A for the design-loop D calculation.
Acceleration distance D (Eq. 1) is implemented as the FOM used for the primary optimization.

Code has been implemented that computes D as the Eq. 1 integral over beta from 0 to beta_final of ((rho_l + rho_s) * c^2 / I) * h(beta) / R(lambda(beta)) d beta, with rho_l (sail areal density) determined from the current design geometry and rho_s from the payload areal density.

The D integrand is evaluated by mapping each beta sample to its Doppler-shifted wavelength lambda(beta) and looking up R(lambda(beta)) from the polarization-averaged reflectivity, with numerical quadrature over beta up to beta_final = 0.2.

For a 200 nm thick unpatterned SiN membrane under the Starshot parameters (I = 10 GW/m^2, lambda_0 = 1.55 um, 10 m^2 sail, 1 g payload), the implemented D evaluates to approximately 67 Gm, matching the red reference line in Fig. 3a.
Acceleration time T (Eq. 2) is implemented as the alternative FOM used for the T-optimization comparison.

Code has been implemented that computes T as the Eq. 2 integral over beta from 0 to beta_final of (m_t * c / (I * A)) * gamma(beta)^3 * (1 - beta) / (1 + beta) / R(lambda(beta)) d beta (or equivalent form consistent with Kulkarni et al. 2018), using the total sail mass m_t and sail area A.

m_t in the T formulation is computed from the current design as rho_SiN * t * Af * A + m_payload, using rho_SiN = 3100 kg/m^3, the optimized thickness t, area fraction Af of the unit cell, and sail area A = 10 m^2.
A direct equation-of-motion integrator consistent with Kulkarni et al. 2018 is implemented so that reflectivity spectra can be turned into velocity(t) and distance(t) curves matching Figs. 3c and 4c.

Code has been implemented that integrates the relativistic equation of motion of the lightsail forward in time given R(lambda), I, A, m_t, and lambda_0, producing beta(t) and position(t) using 300-wavelength reflectivity spectra as specified in Supplementary Section A.

For the same design and parameters, the D obtained by integrating the equation of motion until beta = 0.2 agrees with the Eq. 1 evaluation of D to within 5%, verifying internal consistency of the two computations.

When evaluated on the reported hexagonal and pentagonal designs, the EOM integrator reproduces the ~5 minute difference in acceleration time between them shown in Fig. 3c, with the pentagonal design having the shorter T despite larger D.
The FOM module exposes a differentiable interface that plugs into the neural TO backward pass.

Implement the neural topology optimization pipeline: CNN reparameterization of the design space, post-processing/filtering, RCWA-based functional analysis, and L-BFGS-driven update loop with Area-fraction constraints.
CNN reparameterization: a convolutional neural network maps a randomized latent vector beta into the discretized unit-cell density image that serves as the design representation.

Code has been implemented that defines a convolutional neural network which takes a randomly initialized latent vector beta as input and outputs a 2D image whose spatial dimensions match the discretized unit-cell grid (100x100 for square lattice, 100x172 for hexagonal lattice).
Code has been implemented so that the CNN's trainable weights and biases and the latent vector beta are exposed as optimization variables that can be updated by an external optimizer.
Code has been implemented that initializes beta from a random distribution at the start of every optimization run, producing a random initial material distribution as described in the Methods.
The CNN's forward pass produces pixel values that after post-processing lie in [0, 1] representing the interpolation weight between vacuum and SiN material for every pixel of the design grid.

Design-space geometry and optimization parameters: define the unit-cell shape (square vs hexagonal), thickness t and period Lambda as optimization variables with the correct bounds and initial values.
Code has been implemented that provides both a square lattice unit cell (NxN pixels) and a hexagonal lattice unit cell (N x sqrt(3) N pixels) as selectable design-space shapes, matching Fig. 7b,c.
The unit-cell period Lambda is included as a scalar optimization variable that is constrained to 0.1 um <= Lambda <= 7.2 um and is initialized to lambda_0 = 1.55 um at the start of optimization.
The layer thickness t is included as a scalar optimization variable that is constrained to 0.01 um <= t <= 1 um and initialized to 100 nm at the start of optimization.
Code has been implemented that maps continuous pixel values to a relative permittivity varying between 1 (vacuum) and 4 (SiN) for use in the RCWA solver.
Post-processing / filtering stage: convert the raw CNN output image into a physical density image suitable for the RCWA solver.

Code has been implemented that applies a differentiable post-processing/filtering step to the CNN output image before passing it to the functional analysis stage, in accordance with the four-stage pipeline described in the Methods.
The post-processing step enforces the two-fold rotational/polarization symmetry required so that the resulting design is evaluated identically for phi = 0 and phi = pi/2 orthogonal polarizations.

The neural TO pipeline is implemented WITHOUT the artificial permittivity relaxation factor Q that conventional pixel-based TO requires; the raw filtered density is passed directly to RCWA (Supplementary Section E).
RCWA-based functional analysis: given the discretized unit-cell permittivity, thickness t and period Lambda, compute the reflectivity spectrum R(lambda) required by the figure of merit.

Code has been implemented that calls an RCWA solver on the filtered unit-cell permittivity map, using period Lambda and thickness t, to compute the reflectivity R at a specified wavelength for a normally incident linearly polarized plane wave.

The RCWA call is performed for both orthogonal polarization angles phi = 0 and phi = pi/2 and the reflectivities are averaged (or otherwise combined) so that the optimizer targets a polarization-invariant design.

During optimization the reflectivity spectrum used inside the figure of merit is evaluated at 24 wavelength sample points across the Doppler-shifted band 1.55 um to 1.86 um, matching the paper's stated 24 evaluation points.

Code has been implemented so that the RCWA reflectivity output is differentiable with respect to the CNN outputs and to Lambda and t, so that gradients can propagate back to the optimization variables.
Area-fraction constraint handling: enforce a target material area fraction Af (40-70%) as an optimization constraint used as a proxy for MFS control.
Code has been implemented that computes the Area fraction Af of the current filtered design as the mean material density over the unit cell, in a differentiable manner.

Code has been implemented that adds an Area-fraction constraint (or equivalent penalty) to the optimization so that the converged design achieves a user-specified target Af with values selectable in the 40%-70% range.
When run with a target Af of 55% using the pentagonal-lattice settings, the converged design achieves an Area fraction within a small tolerance (<= 3 percentage points) of the 55% target.

Running the pipeline WITHOUT the Area-fraction constraint reproduces the qualitative observation that the optimized designs follow conventional square or hexagonal hole lattices with sub-500 nm MFS (Fig. 2b,c).
L-BFGS optimizer loop: use L-BFGS to update the CNN weights, beta, Lambda and t by backpropagating gradients of the figure of merit.

Code has been implemented that uses the L-BFGS optimizer (Nocedal 1980) to update all trainable variables of the CNN, the latent vector beta, and the scalars Lambda and t simultaneously at each iteration.

Code has been implemented that performs the forward step (beta -> CNN -> post-processing -> RCWA -> FOM) and computes gradients of the FOM with respect to every trainable variable via automatic differentiation in the backward step.
The optimization loop terminates when either a pre-set relative tolerance on the FOM is reached or a pre-set maximum iteration count is exceeded, and these stopping criteria are user-configurable.
Code has been implemented that logs the FOM value and Area fraction at every iteration so that convergence curves comparable to Supplementary Fig. S4a can be produced.

End-to-end pipeline integration and configurability: the four stages (CNN, post-processing, RCWA, FOM+optimizer) are chained into a single runnable optimization exposing all the paper's key hyperparameters.

Code has been implemented that exposes a single entry-point function/script which accepts lattice type (square/hexagonal), target Area fraction, FOM choice (D or T), and Starshot mission parameters, and returns the converged design image, Lambda, and t.
The pipeline is deterministic given a fixed random seed for beta initialization and CNN weight initialization, so that repeated runs with the same seed yield the same converged design.
Code has been implemented that saves the final converged unit-cell design image (as a binary/greyscale array) along with the final scalar values of Lambda, t and Af to disk for downstream analysis.

When the full pipeline is run with the pentagonal-lattice settings (Af ~ 55%, t = 0.18 um, hexagonal design space, D as FOM), the resulting design converges to a pentagonal-lattice pattern qualitatively matching Fig. 2d.
Reproduce the neural TO designs obtained without an Area fraction constraint, yielding square and hexagonal lattice PhCs (Fig. 2b,c) with reported thicknesses.
Configure the neural TO run for the unconstrained square lattice case with the correct design-space discretization and parameter bounds.
Code has been implemented to set up a square lattice unit cell optimization with a 100×100 pixel design grid, per the methods description.
Code has been implemented so that the square lattice optimization runs without any Area fraction (Af) constraint added to the objective/loss.
Code has been implemented to treat thickness t (bounded 0.01–1 µm) and period Λ (bounded 0.1–7.2 µm) as trainable parameters in the square lattice run, initialized to t=100 nm and Λ=λ0=1.55 µm.
Code has been implemented so that the square lattice optimization uses D (acceleration distance, Eq. 1) as the figure of merit and averages over the two orthogonal polarizations ϕ=0 and ϕ=π/2.
Configure the neural TO run for the unconstrained hexagonal lattice case with the correct hexagonal design-space discretization.
Code has been implemented to set up a hexagonal lattice unit cell with a 100×172 pixel design grid corresponding to an N×√3·N discretization.
Code has been implemented to enforce hexagonal-lattice symmetry/periodicity on the unit cell (e.g. rhombic primitive cell with 60°/120° vectors) so that the resulting design tiles as a hexagonal PhC.
Code has been implemented so that the hexagonal lattice optimization runs without any Area fraction (Af) constraint added to the loss.
Verify that the unconstrained optimizations produce the reported conventional square-lattice and hexagonal-lattice hole patterns shown in Fig. 2b and Fig. 2c.

The optimized square-lattice design has been produced and, after binarization, shows a single-hole-per-unit-cell pattern consistent with a conventional square lattice as in Fig. 2b (black=SiN, white=vacuum).
The optimized hexagonal-lattice design has been produced and, after binarization, shows the honeycomb/hexagonal hole arrangement of Fig. 2c.
Verify the reported optimized thicknesses for the two unconstrained lattice designs.
The optimized thickness of the square-lattice design matches the reported value of 0.2 µm (200 nm).
The optimized thickness of the hexagonal-lattice design matches the reported value of 0.3 µm (300 nm).
Verify that the unconstrained designs fall short of the 500 nm MFS target, consistent with the paper's claim motivating the Af-constrained runs.
Code has been implemented to compute a minimum feature size metric from the binarized unit-cell image of each optimized design.
The computed MFS of both the unconstrained square and hexagonal lattice designs is below 500 nm, matching the paper's statement that these designs do not meet the MFS>500 nm objective.
Evaluate the acceleration performance of the unconstrained designs and confirm they lie on the low-MFS end of the D-vs-MFS curve shown in Fig. 3a.
Code has been implemented to compute the acceleration distance D of the optimized square- and hexagonal-lattice designs using the full reflectivity spectrum over the Doppler band (1.55–1.86 µm).

The computed acceleration distances D for the unconstrained square and hexagonal lattice designs are lower than that of the pentagonal Af=55% design and of the 200 nm unpatterned SiN membrane, consistent with the leftmost points of Fig. 3a.
Reproduce the pentagonal lattice PhC design obtained under Area fraction constraints (40-70%), including the Af=55%, t=0.18 µm reference design (Fig. 2d).
The Area-fraction constraint is correctly formulated and incorporated into the neural TO pipeline for pentagonal-lattice optimization.
Code has been implemented to compute the Area fraction Af of the discretized unit-cell design (fraction of pixels assigned to SiN vs vacuum) from the post-processed CNN output.

Code has been implemented to add an Area-fraction constraint term to the neural TO objective (following Hoyer et al.-style penalty) that drives the design toward a user-specified target Af in the 40-70% range.
The Area-fraction constraint behaves correctly: when a target Af (e.g., 55%) is set, the converged design's measured Af matches the target to within a few percent absolute deviation.
The pentagonal-lattice unit-cell design space and its discretization are correctly configured for neural TO.
Code has been implemented to define a pentagonal-lattice unit-cell design space with appropriate lattice vectors so that periodic tiling produces the observed pentagonal hole arrangement (Fig. 2d).

The pentagonal unit cell is discretized with a pixel grid consistent with the paper (comparable in resolution to the 100x100 / 100x172 grids used for square/hexagonal lattices) and pixel dielectric constants are continuously varied between vacuum (epsilon=1) and SiN (epsilon=4).
The period Lambda and thickness t are treated as trainable optimization parameters constrained to 0.1 um <= Lambda <= 7.2 um and 0.01 um <= t <= 1 um, matching the paper's optimization bounds.
The Af-constrained neural TO run for the pentagonal reference design is executed with the correct optimization protocol.

Code has been implemented to run the neural TO optimization for the pentagonal lattice with the acceleration-distance D as the objective, two orthogonal polarizations (phi=0 and phi=pi/2), and the Af constraint enabled.
The optimization is run for each target Af value in the 40%-70% range (at least Af = 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 70%) to produce the sweep of pentagonal designs used in Fig. 3.
The initial thickness is set to 100 nm, the initial period to lambda_0 = 1.55 um, and the initial material distribution is randomized, as specified in the Methods section.
The Af=55% pentagonal reference design (Fig. 2d) is reproduced with the expected geometric properties.

Code has been implemented to export the converged Af=55% pentagonal design as a binarized unit-cell image plus lattice vectors, matching the visual pattern shown in Fig. 2d (multiple hole shapes/sizes arranged on a pentagonal lattice).
The converged reference pentagonal design has thickness t = 0.18 um, matching the Fig. 2d caption value (within +/- 0.01 um).
The converged reference pentagonal design has an Area fraction of approximately 55% (within +/- 3 percentage points).
The converged reference pentagonal design has a period Lambda consistent with the fabricated 3.0 um pentagonal pattern (Fig. 5 caption), i.e. Lambda ~= 3.0 um within roughly +/- 0.3 um.

The Af=55% pentagonal design contains multiple hole sizes/shapes per unit cell (not a single repeated hole), as emphasized in the Computational Results section describing the broadband multi-peak behavior.
The optical performance of the Af=55% pentagonal reference design matches the paper's reported values.
Code has been implemented to compute the polarization-averaged reflectivity spectrum R(lambda) of the reference pentagonal design over the Doppler band 1.55-1.86 um using the RCWA solver.

The reflectivity spectrum of the Af=55% pentagonal reference design exhibits multiple resonance peaks spread across the Doppler-shifted wavelength range (rather than a single narrow peak), reproducing the qualitative pentagonal-lattice spectrum shown in Fig. 3b.

The acceleration distance D of the Af=55% pentagonal reference design, computed via Eq. (1) with the Starshot parameters, matches the value plotted for this design in Fig. 3a (pentagonal point near MFS ~500 nm) within ~15%.

The pentagonal reference design accelerates the sail to 0.2c approximately 5 minutes faster than the corresponding hexagonal design in Fig. 3c, reproducing the reported ~5 min pentagonal-vs-hexagonal launch-time gap (within ~1 min).
The pentagonal reference design satisfies the MFS > 500 nm objective (minimum distance between holes and minimum feature width both >= 500 nm) as measured on the binarized converged geometry.
Reproduce Fig. 3a–c: acceleration distance D versus MFS for square/hexagonal/pentagonal designs, reflectivity spectra over the Doppler band, and velocity-vs-time curves.
Assemble the ensemble of optimized PhC unit cells (square, hexagonal, and pentagonal-lattice designs) needed to populate the D-vs-MFS sweep of Fig. 3a.

Code has been implemented that collects, for each Area-fraction constraint in the 40–70% range (plus the unconstrained square and hexagonal designs), the optimized geometry (pixel grid, period Λ, thickness t) into a design table used for the Fig. 3a sweep.
Code has been implemented that computes the minimum feature size (MFS) of each design in the sweep (e.g., minimum distance between hole edges) and associates it with that design.
Code has been implemented that includes the reference 200 nm thick unpatterned SiN membrane as a baseline entry in the D-vs-MFS dataset.
Compute high-resolution reflectivity spectra R(λ) over the full Doppler band 1.55–1.86 µm for each design in the sweep.
Code has been implemented that evaluates the RCWA reflectivity of each optimized unit cell at 300 wavelengths spanning 1.55–1.86 µm, averaging over the two orthogonal polarizations ϕ=0 and ϕ=π/2.

The computed reflectivity spectra include (near-)zero reflectivity outside resonance peaks and one or more sharp resonance peaks whose center wavelengths fall inside the 1.55–1.86 µm Doppler window for the hexagonal and pentagonal designs (Fig. 3b).

The pentagonal design's reflectivity spectrum exhibits multiple resonance peaks of relatively lower peak reflectivity spread across the Doppler band, while the hexagonal design shows fewer, higher-reflectivity peaks, matching the qualitative behavior of Fig. 3b.
Integrate the relativistic equation of motion to obtain velocity-vs-time and distance-vs-time curves for each candidate lightsail design (Fig. 3c).

Code has been implemented that numerically integrates the lightsail equation of motion (Kulkarni et al.) using the full R(λ) spectrum, mapping the Doppler-shifted wavelength λ(β)=λ0·sqrt((1+β)/(1−β)) to the appropriate reflectivity at each timestep.

The integrator uses the Starshot mission parameters (I=10 GW/m², sail area 10 m², total mass consistent with the mission spec, target β=0.2) and terminates at β=0.2 to report acceleration time T and travelled distance D.
Code has been implemented that produces velocity-vs-time curves for the hexagonal and pentagonal PhC designs from Fig. 3, plotted against the speed-of-light asymptote as in Fig. 3c.
Produce the Fig. 3a plot showing D as a function of MFS for the different lattice families and verify the reported quantitative trends.

Code has been implemented that plots D (Gm) versus MFS (nm) with distinct markers/colors for square, hexagonal, and pentagonal lattice designs, plus a horizontal reference line at the D of the 200 nm unpatterned SiN membrane.
The plotted D increases monotonically (within noise) with increasing MFS across the pentagonal-lattice family (Af 40–70%), reproducing the trend in Fig. 3a.
The 200 nm unpatterned SiN reference gives D ≈ 67 Gm as stated in the text and shown in Fig. 3a (red line).
The best unconstrained square-lattice design (MFS below 500 nm) reproduces the D value shown for it in Fig. 3a within tolerance.
The best unconstrained hexagonal-lattice design reproduces the D value plotted in Fig. 3a within tolerance.
The Af=55%, t=0.18 µm pentagonal design (Fig. 2d / Fig. 3) meets the MFS>500 nm objective and reproduces its Fig. 3a D value within tolerance.
Produce the Fig. 3b reflectivity-spectrum panel for the selected designs and verify numerical agreement with the paper.
Code has been implemented that plots R(λ) over 1.55–1.86 µm for the selected square, hexagonal, and pentagonal designs on a single axis matching the layout of Fig. 3b.
The peak reflectivity of the selected hexagonal design's principal resonance is close to 98–99% (single-layer PhC narrowband peak) and its FWHM matches Fig. 3b within tolerance.
The pentagonal design's Doppler-band-averaged reflectivity ⟨R⟩ over 1.55–1.86 µm matches the value implied by Fig. 3b within tolerance.
Produce the Fig. 3c velocity-vs-time comparison and verify the reported acceleration-time gap between hexagonal and pentagonal designs.
Code has been implemented that plots v(t)/c for the selected hexagonal and pentagonal PhC lightsails on the same axes as in Fig. 3c, terminating at β=0.2.
The reproduced acceleration time T for the selected hexagonal design matches the value shown in Fig. 3c within tolerance.
The reproduced acceleration time T for the selected pentagonal design matches the Fig. 3c value within tolerance.
The difference in acceleration time between the hexagonal and pentagonal designs equals approximately 5 minutes (pentagonal faster), as stated in the text describing Fig. 3c.
The reproduced curves demonstrate that the pentagonal design has both larger D and lower T than the hexagonal design in Fig. 3a/c, confirming the non-monotonic D–T relation highlighted by the paper.
Reproduce Fig. 4: designs and acceleration curves obtained when optimizing for acceleration time T versus distance D, including the ~6 minute launch-time reduction and reflectivity peak shift.
Configure and run the T-optimization experiments producing the designs shown in Fig. 4b.

Code has been implemented to switch the neural TO optimization objective between figure of merit D (acceleration distance, Eq. 1) and figure of merit T (acceleration time, Eq. 2) via a single configuration flag, while keeping all other pipeline components (CNN, RCWA, L-BFGS, mission parameters) unchanged.

Code has been implemented to run the T-optimization on a hexagonal lattice unit cell (100 x 172 pixel grid) under the Area-fraction constraint window that yields an MFS >= 500 nm design, using the same initialization protocol (random material distribution, initial thickness 100 nm, initial period lambda_0) as the D-optimization runs.

Code has been implemented to run the T-optimization on a pentagonal lattice unit cell under Area-fraction constraints in the 40-70% range, matching the setup used for the D-optimized pentagonal design in Fig. 3.

The hexagonal PhC design obtained by T-optimization exhibits a hexagonal lattice arrangement of holes (as shown blue in Fig. 4b), distinct from the pentagonal lattice, and satisfies the MFS >= 500 nm objective.
The pentagonal PhC design obtained by T-optimization retains the pentagonal lattice topology (as shown green in Fig. 4b) similar to the D-optimized pentagonal design.
Compute reflectivity spectra and acceleration trajectories for the T-optimized vs D-optimized designs (Fig. 4a, 4c).

Code has been implemented to compute the broadband reflectivity spectrum (via RCWA, averaged over phi=0 and phi=pi/2 polarizations) across the full Doppler-shifted wavelength range 1.55-1.86 um using at least 300 evaluation points for both the D-optimized and T-optimized hexagonal designs, as plotted in Fig. 4a.

Code has been implemented to numerically integrate the lightsail equation of motion (Kulkarni et al. formulation) using the computed reflectivity spectrum, producing velocity-vs-time trajectories up to the final target velocity beta = 0.2 for the Starshot mission parameters.

Code has been implemented to reproduce Fig. 4c: a plot of sail velocity (as fraction of c) versus acceleration time for both the T-optimized hexagonal and T-optimized pentagonal designs, with shaded regions I and II highlighting how the initial reflectivity spectrum translates to initial acceleration.

Code has been implemented to reproduce Fig. 4a: an overlaid reflectivity-vs-wavelength plot of the D-optimized and T-optimized hexagonal designs, annotated with an arrow indicating the leftward (toward laser wavelength) shift of the reflectivity peak when optimizing for T.
Verify the quantitative claims comparing T-optimized and D-optimized hexagonal designs.

The reflectivity peak of the T-optimized hexagonal design is shifted toward the laser wavelength (1.55 um, left side of the Doppler band) relative to the D-optimized hexagonal design's peak, as depicted by the red arrow in Fig. 4a.

The acceleration time T of the T-optimized hexagonal design is approximately 6 minutes shorter than that of the D-optimized hexagonal design when integrated under Starshot mission parameters (I = 10 GW/m^2, lambda_0 = 1.55 um, sail area 10 m^2, target beta = 0.2).
The T-optimized hexagonal design exhibits a larger acceleration distance D than the D-optimized hexagonal design, confirming the D-vs-T tradeoff described for the hexagonal lattice.

The 6-minute reduction in T translates, using the paper's cost model (10 GW/m^2 laser on 10 m^2 sail, 0.185 EUR/kWh electricity price, ideal energy/momentum conversion), to a launch-cost saving of approximately 2 million euros per launch.

For the pentagonal lattice, the values of D and T obtained when optimizing for T versus optimizing for D are approximately equal (no significant performance change), confirming the paper's statement that pentagonal designs are insensitive to the D-vs-T objective choice.

The T-optimized hexagonal and T-optimized pentagonal velocity-vs-time curves in Fig. 4c follow closely similar trajectories, supporting the claim that neural TO finds a basin of designs with comparable T outcomes.
Present and log the T-vs-D comparison outputs.

Code has been implemented to save, for each of the four designs (D-opt hexagonal, T-opt hexagonal, D-opt pentagonal, T-opt pentagonal), the final unit-cell binary image, period Lambda, thickness t, Area fraction, MFS, D, and T to disk in a reproducible tabular format.
Code has been implemented to render Fig. 4b: side-by-side binary images of the T-optimized hexagonal (blue-tinted) and T-optimized pentagonal (green-tinted) unit-cell designs.
Reproduce the cost and launch-time analysis quantifying manufacturing and launch cost differences based on lithography throughput and acceleration-time savings.
Implement lithography throughput and manufacturing cost analysis comparing e-beam vs i-line optical lithography.
Code has been implemented that encodes the lithography throughput assumptions: e-beam writing rate of 7.5e-5 m^2/hr and i-line optical lithography writing rate of 0.43 m^2/hr for a 10 m^2 sail area.
Code has been implemented that encodes the cleanroom operating cost of ~200 euro/hr used to convert writing time into manufacturing cost per sail.
Code computes the e-beam writing time for a 10 m^2 sail and returns approximately 15 years, matching the paper's reported value.
Code computes the i-line optical lithography writing time for a 10 m^2 sail and returns approximately one day (~23 hours), matching the paper.
Code computes the e-beam manufacturing cost per 10 m^2 sail and returns approximately 26 million euros.
Code computes the i-line optical lithography manufacturing cost per 10 m^2 sail and returns approximately 3,000 euros.
Code computes the ratio of e-beam to i-line manufacturing cost per sail and reports a reduction factor of approximately 9000x.
Implement launch-cost analysis based on laser energy consumption and acceleration time.
Code has been implemented that encodes the electricity price of 0.185 euro/kWh (Eurostat 2023 non-household average) used for launch-cost estimation.
Code has been implemented that computes launch energy as laser intensity (10 GW/m^2) times sail area (10 m^2) times acceleration time T, assuming ideal energy conversion and ideal momentum transfer.
Code computes the total launch cost for a nominal lightsail acceleration and returns approximately 9.3 million euros as the reference total launch cost cited in the paper.
Code computes the launch-cost difference associated with the ~5 minute acceleration-time reduction between the pentagonal and hexagonal designs (Fig. 3c) and returns approximately 1.5 million euros.
Code computes the launch-cost difference associated with the ~6 minute reduction in acceleration time when optimizing for T versus D (Fig. 4) and returns approximately 2 million euros per launch.

Code computes the aggregated per-sail savings combining the ~9000x manufacturing cost reduction and the acceleration-time-driven launch-cost savings, and reports a total budget reduction approaching 25 million euros per lightsail as stated in the Discussion.
Produce reporting/analysis outputs summarizing the cost comparisons.
Code produces a summary table or printout comparing e-beam vs i-line optical lithography for the 10 m^2 sail, including writing rate, total writing time, cost per sail, and cost-reduction factor.
Code produces a summary of per-launch cost as a function of acceleration time T, evaluated for the pentagonal and hexagonal designs from Figs. 3-4, exposing the 1.5M and 2M euro differentials.
Reproduce Supplementary Section D ablation on total-mass constraints (1 g, 2.5 g, larger), showing manufacturability limits and reflectivity trade-offs across the three cases.
Mass constraint integrated into the neural TO pipeline as an additional optimization constraint controlling total sail mass across thickness and Area fraction.
Code has been implemented to compute the total sail mass as m_t = rho_SiN * A_sail * t * Af, using SiN density 3100 kg/m^3 and sail area 10 m^2, where Af is derived from the design pixel grid.

Code has been implemented to add a mass-equality (or upper-bound) constraint m_t <= M_target to the neural TO objective, with configurable M_target values of 1 g, 2.5 g, and a larger value (~3 g) corresponding to the pentagonal design of Fig. 3.
Code has been implemented to jointly optimize thickness t and Area fraction Af under the mass constraint, allowing t and Af to trade off while keeping m_t at the specified value.
Three mass-constraint cases (1 g, 2.5 g, and larger ~3 g) are separately optimized and their resulting designs are produced as per Supplementary Fig. S3a.

Case 1 (1 g constraint) optimization is run and the resulting design is saved and rendered; the design must exhibit freely suspended (disconnected) mass regions demonstrating non-manufacturability as described in Supplementary Section D.
Case 2 (2.5 g constraint) optimization produces a design consisting of parallel strings of material (string-like/1D-periodic pattern), consistent with Supplementary Fig. S3a case 2.
Case 3 (larger mass ~3 g) optimization yields the pentagonal lattice PhC design that is viable for manufacturing, matching Supplementary Fig. S3a case 3.
A manufacturability check flags Case 1 as containing disconnected (floating) material components and Cases 2/3 as connected, using a connected-components analysis on the binarized design.
Reflectivity spectra and acceleration curves for the three mass-constraint cases are computed and reproduced in the style of Supplementary Fig. S3b,c.
Code has been implemented to compute the reflectivity spectrum R(lambda) across the full Doppler-shifted band (1.55-1.86 um) for each of the three mass-constrained designs using the RCWA solver.
Code has been implemented to integrate the equation of motion to produce velocity-vs-time (acceleration) curves for the three cases, reproducing Supplementary Fig. S3c.
Case 3 (the pentagonal design) exhibits the highest reflectivity across the laser wavelength band among the three cases, as claimed in Supplementary Fig. S3b.

Case 3 has the lowest acceleration time T among the three mass-constraint cases, while Case 2 yields the shortest acceleration distance D, consistent with the ordering reported in Supplementary Fig. S3.
The reproduced pentagonal (Case 3) design has a total mass of approximately 3 g for a 10 m^2 sail, matching the value stated in Supplementary Section D.
Reproduce Supplementary Section E ablation comparing neural TO to conventional pixel-based MMA topology optimization, with and without the relaxation factor Q (Fig. S4).
Implement the conventional pixel-based topology optimization baseline for comparison.

Code has been implemented for a pixel-based topology optimization model where each pixel in a 100×100 (or 100×172 hexagonal) design grid is a directly optimized continuous design variable representing material fraction between vacuum and SiN.
Code has been implemented that uses the Method of Moving Asymptotes (MMA) from the NLopt library as the optimizer for the pixel-based topology optimization baseline.

The pixel-based TO baseline uses the same RCWA forward solver, mission parameters, acceleration-distance objective, and unit-cell geometry (3.0 µm periodicity, 200 nm thickness) as the neural TO pipeline so results are directly comparable.
Implement the relaxation factor Q used to smooth the optimization landscape and enable running both models with and without Q.

Code has been implemented for the relaxation factor Q as described in Jin et al. (ACS Photonics 2020) that artificially relaxes the permittivity/reflectivity contributions during the RCWA-based optimization so the pixel-based TO can converge smoothly.

The optimization driver exposes a toggle to enable or disable the relaxation factor Q, so that all four ablation configurations (Pixel with Q, Pixel without Q, Neural with Q, Neural without Q) can be run from the same codebase.
Run and log the four ablation configurations on the fabricated pentagonal unit cell (3.0 µm period, 200 nm thickness) reported in Fig. S4.

Code has been implemented to execute the four ablation runs (Pixel+Q, Pixel−Q, Neural+Q, Neural−Q) on the same unit cell with periodicity 3.0 µm and thickness 200 nm, using consistent random seeds/initializations across methods.
Code has been implemented to log the objective value (loss) at every optimization iteration for each of the four runs and to save the final design images, matching the data shown in Fig. S4a–e.
Code has been implemented to reproduce Fig. S4a: a loss-versus-iteration plot overlaying the four ablation curves (Pixel with/without Q, Neural with/without Q).
Verify the qualitative claims of the ablation from Fig. S4b–e.
With the relaxation factor Q enabled, the pixel-based TO (Fig. S4b) and neural TO (Fig. S4c) both converge to visually similar pentagonal-lattice-like designs with comparable final objective values.

Without the relaxation factor Q, the pixel-based TO (Fig. S4d) fails to converge to a good solution (the design remains essentially unchanged over more than 100 iterations), while the neural TO (Fig. S4e) still converges to a good pentagonal-like design.

The neural TO without relaxation factor achieves a final objective value that is lower (better) than the pixel-based TO with relaxation factor on the same 3.0 µm / 200 nm unit cell, as claimed in Supplementary Section E.

The neural TO ablation runs demonstrate robustness in the sense that no substantial hyperparameter tuning is required to obtain the reported convergence behaviour, matching the qualitative claim in Supplementary Section E.

Reproduce the polarization-sweep analysis (Supplementary Fig. S1c) showing acceleration distance D versus incident polarization angle φ for the square, hexagonal, and pentagonal lattice designs, demonstrating the polarization sensitivity of each design.
Implement the polarization sweep procedure that evaluates D as a function of incident polarization angle for a fixed optimized unit cell.

Code has been implemented to compute the reflectivity spectrum of a fixed PhC unit cell for a single linearly polarized normally-incident plane wave with a variable polarization angle φ in the crystal plane, using RCWA.

Code has been implemented to sweep φ from 0 to π across a discrete set of angles (covering at least ~10 points spanning [0, π]) and, for each angle, evaluate the full acceleration distance D via the same Eq. (1) integral used elsewhere in the paper.
Code has been implemented that generates a plot of D versus φ for the square, hexagonal, and pentagonal designs on the same axes, reproducing Supplementary Fig. S1c.
Verify that each design's D vs φ curve satisfies the qualitative and quantitative behavior reported in Supplementary Fig. S1c.
The hexagonal-lattice design's D varies negligibly across φ ∈ [0, π] (approximately polarization-invariant), consistent with Supplementary Fig. S1c.

The square-lattice design's D degrades substantially (approaching loss of performance) for φ in the range roughly between 0.5π and π, reproducing the strong polarization dependence shown in Supplementary Fig. S1c.
The pentagonal-lattice design's D vs φ curve reproduces the intermediate polarization dependence shown in Supplementary Fig. S1c, remaining bounded and non-vanishing across the full angular range.

At φ = 0 and φ = π/2 (the two angles used during optimization), each of the three designs reproduces the D value shown in Supplementary Fig. S1a/S1c within reported tolerance, confirming consistency between the polarization sweep and the primary D-vs-MFS results.

The ratio of maximum to minimum D over the swept angles for the square lattice is substantially larger than that of the hexagonal lattice, quantitatively confirming the polarization-sensitivity ordering (square ≫ pentagonal ≥ hexagonal) reported in Supplementary Fig. S1c.
Code has been implemented to save the numerical D(φ) traces for all three lattices to a machine-readable file (e.g. CSV or NPZ) for downstream analysis and reproducibility.
Reproduce the fabrication process for the 60×60 mm² 200 nm thick suspended SiN pentagonal PhC membrane, including LPCVD, i-line stepper lithography, C2F6 ICP etch, and cryogenic SF6 undercut steps.
Prepare the starting Si wafer with LPCVD-grown SiN as specified.
Fabrication uses a 100 mm diameter silicon wafer as the starting substrate.
Code/process has been implemented to deposit a 200 nm thick silicon nitride layer via low-pressure chemical vapour deposition (LPCVD) on the Si wafer.
The LPCVD SiN film exhibits a tensile pre-stress of approximately 270 MPa (as measured on the deposited film).
Apply and process the AZ ECI 3012 positive-tone photoresist stack before exposure.
A HMDS priming step is performed at 130 °C for 30 s prior to resist coating.
A dehydration/bake step at 130 °C for 60 s is performed prior to resist spin coating.
AZ ECI 3012 positive-tone photoresist is used as the lithography mask material.
Resist is spin coated at 6850 rpm to achieve a target film thickness of 1 µm.
Resist is soft-baked at 95 °C for 150 s after spin coating.
Perform i-line stepper lithography to pattern the pentagonal PhC across a 60×60 mm² area.
Exposure is performed on an ASML PAS 5500/80 automatic wafer stepper (i-line, 365 nm source).
The resist is exposed with a dose of 110 mJ/cm².
A chrome-on-quartz reticle is used encoding the pentagonal PhC unit cell design with 3.0 µm period.
The stepper stitches 5×5 mm² field patterns together to form the full 60×60 mm² PhC membrane pattern.
The lithography process achieves a minimum feature size >500 nm as targeted by the i-line stepper's diffraction-limited resolution.
Post-exposure development sequence for the resist mask.
A post-exposure bake (PEB) is performed at 115 °C for 150 s.
Single-puddle development is performed using MF322 developer for 60 s at 3000 rpm.
The developed resist is hard-baked at 100 °C for 150 s prior to plasma etching.
Directional ICP etch of the SiN layer followed by cryogenic SF6 undercut to suspend the membrane.
A directional inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etch with C2F6 chemistry is performed for 60 s to transfer the resist pattern through the 200 nm SiN layer.
The photoresist mask is removed after the SiN etch and before the undercut step.
A fluorine-based SF6 ICP etch is performed at -120 °C for 45 s to isotropically undercut the Si beneath the patterned SiN and suspend the PhC membrane.
The cryogenic temperature (-120 °C) is used to enhance SiN/Si selectivity of the SF6 etch, keeping the SiN membrane intact while removing underlying Si.
The undercut proceeds such that the membrane releases from the edges first and the center last, maintaining thermal anchoring of the center during release.
Characterize final device geometry against paper specifications.
The final suspended pentagonal PhC membrane has lateral dimensions of 60×60 mm² on a 100 mm wafer.
The final suspended SiN membrane has a thickness of approximately 200 nm after all fabrication steps.
The fabricated pentagonal lattice has a period of 3.0 µm as designed.
The finished membrane contains approximately 1.5 billion nanoscale holes across the 60×60 mm² pentagonal pattern.
The device achieves a lateral-length to thickness aspect ratio of approximately 3×10^5 (60 mm / 200 nm).
Post-fabrication SEM analysis shows edge holes are approximately 3% larger than center holes due to the etch-loading effect during the SF6 undercut.

Reproduce the tunable-laser reflectivity measurement of the fabricated 60×60 mm² pentagonal PhC membrane over 1530–1620 nm against a silver reference, and generate the measured spectrum shown in Fig. 6c.
The reflectivity measurement optical setup is implemented/described in code or configuration matching Fig. 6a topology.
Code has been implemented that specifies a tunable laser source with a sweep range from 1530 nm to 1620 nm as the illumination source for the reflectivity measurement.
Code has been implemented that models/records the fiber path from the tunable laser through a circulator, polarization controller (PC), and collimator into free space, matching the setup in Fig. 6a.
Code has been implemented that includes a linear polarizer after the collimator to ensure the free-space beam incident on the sample is linearly polarized.
Code has been implemented that specifies a lens set and objective to focus/reduce the beam size onto the PhC membrane at normal incidence.
Code has been implemented that routes reflected light back through the same optical path, diverted by the circulator through an attenuator to a photodetector for signal acquisition.
Measurement acquisition and normalization procedures are implemented.
Code has been implemented that performs a signal-maximization/alignment step on a silver mirror reference at 1580 nm prior to sweeping the reflectivity spectrum.
Code has been implemented that records photodetector response versus wavelength across 1530–1620 nm for both the silver reference and the PhC membrane.

Code has been implemented that normalizes the PhC photodetector spectrum by the silver mirror photodetector spectrum and multiplies by the known reflectivity spectrum of silver to obtain the absolute reflectivity of the PhC.
Code has been implemented that only captures the normally reflected, zero-order diffracted component consistent with the setup's collection geometry described in the Methods.
Sample handling and mounting for the fabricated wafer are addressed.
Code/procedure has been implemented that mounts the 100 mm diameter wafer holding the 60×60 mm² suspended pentagonal PhC membrane in the measurement setup as depicted in Fig. 6b.
Code has been implemented that aligns the focused beam to the suspended membrane region (away from silicon-supported areas) for reflectivity measurement.
The measured reflectivity spectrum matches the reported data in Fig. 6c.
The measured reflectivity spectrum spans 1530–1620 nm with wavelength sampling sufficient to resolve the resonance features shown in Fig. 6c.
The measured reflectivity spectrum from the fabricated pentagonal PhC agrees with the values plotted in Fig. 6c (orange curve) within reported experimental uncertainty across 1530–1620 nm.

The wavelength location of the primary reflectivity resonance peak in the measured spectrum matches the peak position shown in Fig. 6c within the 10–20 nm shift range attributed to hole-size non-uniformity.

sub_tasks.requirements: Reproduce the RCWA simulation of the as-fabricated PhC (including Si substrate, vacuum gap, and roughness layer per Fig. 6d and Supplementary Fig. S2) and demonstrate agreement with the measured zero-order reflectivity.
Build the extended RCWA simulation stack that models the fabricated device (SiN PhC membrane + vacuum gap + Si substrate + roughness layer) as depicted in Fig. 6d.

Code has been implemented that constructs a multi-layer RCWA stack consisting of (from top to bottom): vacuum superstrate, patterned SiN PhC layer, vacuum gap layer, roughness layer, and Si substrate.

Code has been implemented that assigns the SiN patterned layer's in-plane pattern from a scanning electron microscope (SEM)-derived binary image of the fabricated pentagonal unit cell rather than the nominal optimized design.

Code has been implemented that sets the roughness layer's effective relative permittivity via the Bruggeman/linear mixing rule ε_rough = ε_Si · vf + ε_SiN · (1 − vf), following Fujiwara's roughness treatment referenced by the paper.

Code has been implemented that exposes h_gap (vacuum gap height), t_PhC (SiN membrane thickness), t_rough (roughness layer thickness), and vf (roughness volume fraction) as adjustable parameters of the simulation, matching the fit variables in Supplementary Fig. S2.

Code has been implemented that extracts only the zero-order (specularly reflected, normally back-propagating) diffraction efficiency from the RCWA solution, since the measurement setup collects only zero-order light.
Configure physical and numerical parameters of the fabricated-device simulation consistent with the Methods description.
Code has been implemented that sweeps the incident wavelength across the tunable-laser range 1530–1620 nm at normal incidence for the fabricated-device simulation.
The fabricated unit cell used for simulation has a pentagonal-lattice period of 3.0 µm (matching the fabricated device described in Fig. 5a) and a nominal SiN thickness of 200 nm before etch loss.
Code has been implemented that uses ε_SiN = 4 and ε_Si from a standard reference (or a fixed value used in the paper) at 1.55 µm, with vacuum permittivity ε = 1 for the gap.

Code has been implemented that fits h_gap, t_PhC, t_rough, and vf to the measured reflectivity spectrum (e.g., by nonlinear least-squares) and reports the fitted values along with an error band, mirroring Supplementary Fig. S2.
Verify that the fabricated-device simulation reproduces the qualitative and quantitative agreement with the measured zero-order reflectivity shown in Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. S2.
The fitted vacuum-gap height h_gap between the SiN membrane and Si substrate is approximately 4 µm, consistent with the value deduced from optical microscopy of the undercut edge.
The fitted roughness-layer thickness t_rough is approximately 100 nm, matching the value reported in the Methods (Simulation of measurement) section.

The simulated zero-order reflectivity spectrum agrees with the measured spectrum across 1530–1620 nm within the error band shown in Supplementary Fig. S2 (i.e., peak positions align and amplitudes match to within the reported uncertainty).
The simulation confirms that edge holes being ~3% larger than center holes produces a 10–20 nm shift in the reflectivity spectrum, as reported in the Experimental Results section.

Code has been implemented that reproduces Fig. 6c by plotting the SEM-derived fabricated-design simulation (blue) together with the measured reflectivity normalized to the silver-mirror reference (orange).
